name: Virtual power plants and demand flexibility
summary: Software coordinates many batteries, vehicles, thermostats and flexible industrial loads as a resource the electricity grid can dispatch.
useCase: Your home battery exports power during a grid peak and your thermostat briefly shifts demand; an aggregator pays you for participating.
whyNow: There are already commercial VPPs, but aggregation of newer devices and participation in additional markets is still expanding. Wood Mackenzie’s 2025 North America study reported 37.5 GW of behind-the-meter flexible capacity, a 13.7% increase over the preceding study period. Its share of wholesale capacity supplied by residential customers rose from 8.8% in 2024 to 10.2%. This is valuable because grid and generation projects take time, while some flexibility comes from equipment already installed. Nameplate connected devices are not the same as dependable capacity: customer opt-outs, communication failures, baseline rules and simultaneous dispatch determine what a VPP can actually deliver.

mainstream.scope: Routine utility procurement of aggregated residential and commercial flexibility in suitable US, European and Australian electricity markets.
mainstream.rationale: Existing commercial programmes reduce technology risk; market access, device interoperability and dependable dispatch are the remaining scaling tasks. Some regions already meet this definition, while others may not by 2035. Retail tariffs, incentives and utility rules determine the local date more than software maturity.

metric.name: Residential share of North American VPP wholesale-market capacity
metric.scope: Wood Mackenzie study definitions; share of VPP capacity serving wholesale markets, not share of total grid load.
metric.limitations: Changes in surveyed coverage and market participation can affect the share. Show percentage-point change, not CAGR. Total surveyed VPP capacity in 2025 was 37.5 GW, up 13.7%.
metric.futureNote: No defensible comparable external deployment forecast found. The separate maturity path is an analyst scenario, not measured adoption.
metric.growthLabel: +1.4 percentage points residential share; total capacity +13.7%

milestones.text: Commercial demand response pre-dates this window; no consistent whole-market annual VPP value was retained for 2021.
DER aggregation continued through existing programmes; no comparable annual measurement is available in the selected study series.
DOE’s VPP liftoff work described an existing 30–60 GW US base and a possible 80–160 GW 2030 pathway, using a broader definition than Wood Mackenzie.
Residential devices supplied 8.8% of the wholesale-market VPP capacity in Wood Mackenzie’s comparison.
Wood Mackenzie reported 37.5 GW flexible capacity, 13.7% growth, and a residential wholesale share of 10.2%.

Voltus and Octopus announced a February partnership for aggregated devices; Renew Home rebranded to Everyday Electric in October. These are commercial ecosystem changes, not full-year capacity observations.

tailwinds: Flexible demand can relieve peaks without waiting for all new generation and transmission to be built.
Batteries, connected HVAC and EV charging enlarge the pool of dispatchable devices.
Customers can receive payments or lower bills, supporting voluntary enrollment.
bottlenecks: Rules for baselines, telemetry and compensation differ by jurisdiction.
Customers may opt out or prioritise comfort, mobility and backup reserves.
Installed device capacity can overstate simultaneous dependable grid support.
watchMetrics: Verified peak MW delivered and duration during real system stress.
Customer retention, opt-out rates, payments and cost of acquiring an enrolled household.
Contracted utility/wholesale capacity versus merely connected nameplate capacity.
